methodological_rigor.justification: This is a substantial multicenter observational follow-up study with prespecified survival endpoints, explicit exclusion criteria, and a matched SEER reference framework. The manuscript uses appropriate time-to-event methods, competing-risk logic where needed, and one-sample proportional-hazards modeling with profile likelihood and MCMC-based interval estimation for the reference comparisons. Its main limitations are the noninterventional design, residual confounding from unmeasured factors such as health-care access and histologic subtype, and the fact that the analysis cannot fully overcome selection bias inherent to the underlying CCGA cohort.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is best classified as an individual observational cohort study, so Oxford level 2b is appropriate. The clinical relevance is high because the paper addresses how blood-based multicancer detection relates to long-term survival and whether early-stage CSD cancers appear biologically more aggressive than conventionally detected cancers. Even though the study is observational, the findings are directly relevant to screening strategy, prognostic interpretation, and counseling around MCED deployment.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is the right framework because the manuscript reports an observational cohort with longitudinal follow-up, detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria, and a flow-style accounting of participants. The paper is strong on statistical description and shows figures and tables that align with the text, but it does not describe a public data repository, code release, or protocol registration beyond the original study identifier. Reporting is thorough, yet the reproducibility posture remains limited.

novelty_literature.justification: The main novelty is the updated five-year prognostic analysis using the CCGA3 validation substudy and a revised comparison framework against matched SEER survival. That meaningfully extends prior three-year work on the same platform, but it is still an incremental evolution of an established MCED prognostic question rather than a new conceptual advance. The manuscript is well positioned in the literature and avoids strong overclaiming.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written, the abstract is quantitatively grounded, and the results and discussion follow a sensible path from cohort description to stage-stratified survival interpretation. Figure captions are informative and mostly standalone, which helps because the paper relies on several layered survival comparisons. The main writing weakness is that some discussion passages are repetitive, but the overall presentation is strong.

key_strengths: Large longitudinal cohort with five-year follow-up and clear accounting of deaths, survivors, and losses to follow-up.
The SEER-matched reference approach is a thoughtful way to separate signal-detection status from baseline clinical risk.
The analysis is statistically more mature than many observational prognostic papers, with explicit survival modeling and stage-stratified comparisons.
key_concerns: The study is still observational, so residual confounding and healthy-volunteer bias remain plausible explanations for some differences.
Important clinical covariates such as detailed histology, treatment, and health-care access were not fully controlled.
No explicit public data or code release is described.
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a strong observational prognostic paper with good methods and real clinical relevance, but it remains bounded by the limitations of the underlying cohort and reference-matching design. It is suitable for a solid translational oncology journal, with enough rigor for a higher-tier submission after revision.
